title: A room behind the shop
hookLine: keep a room behind the shop, all your own, where true freedom lives (Essays 1.39)
carry: love the front; keep a room behind it

cards: A parked car in the driveway, engine off, with somebody still sitting in it. The groceries can wait three more minutes. So can the people inside.

Or the shower with the fan running, or the long way home from the store: a few minutes nobody else can reach. Montaigne had a spot like that, and a name for it. He didn't take the name from a monastery or a mountain.
He took it from a shop.

teach.b: First, the room. In his essay Of Solitude, Montaigne says we should set aside a back shop, all our own, entirely free, where we keep our true liberty and our main retreat.
Picture a small shop: out front, the counter, the customers, the bell on the door. Behind a curtain, a back room where the shopkeeper sits down.
There, he says, we hold our ordinary talk with ourselves, so privately that nothing from outside gets in. Second, the people out front. This isn't a plan to run away.
Have a spouse, children, goods, and above all health, if we can, he says. Just don't be so tied to them that our happiness hangs on them.

teach.h: LOVE THE FRONT; DON'T LIVE THERE.
teach.b: Love the front of the shop; don't live only there. Third, the trip you can't take. Leaving the crowd, he says, isn't enough on its own.
We carry our worries and wants with us, even into the quietest place. Moving to the country doesn't empty the mind.
The retreat has to happen inside, or it doesn't happen. Fourth, belonging to yourself. In the same essay he writes that the greatest thing in the world is knowing how to belong to yourself.
Not to your job, not to your reputation, not even, all the way down, to the people you love most. Last week we met his tower. The tower was a building.
The back shop is portable: ten minutes, a closed door, and nothing to produce.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take the back shop as a daily habit: a short, protected stretch of time, kept free even in a full life of family and work.

o: a hermit's cell, far away from family and every duty
a storeroom where a merchant hides his finest goods
a private inner room of your own, kept free inside you

p: keep them; don't hang on them
knowing how to belong to yourself

s: Montaigne tells readers to give up family and goods for solitude
he says to have them if we can, just not to let our happiness hang on them.
he says going somewhere quiet isn't enough on its own
we carry our worries with us; the retreat has to happen inside.
the back shop is a place for talking with yourself
he says we hold our ordinary talk with ourselves there, so privately nothing from outside gets in.

games.q: you have a family, a job and a house, and you want what Montaigne calls true liberty. what does he advise?
o: leave it all for a life apart.
keep them, and keep a back room in yourself that doesn't depend on them.
work harder now so you can be free later.
games.why: he says to have spouse, children and goods if we can, but to set aside a back shop, all our own, where our freedom lives.

practice: Let the front of the shop go quiet: the phone face down, the list put away. Notice the voices that usually follow you in, a request, a worry, somebody's opinion of you, and let each one wait at the counter.
Behind the curtain is a small room where nobody needs anything from you; sit in it and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The back shop. Montaigne's room behind the counter, all our own, where we keep our freedom and talk with ourselves. Today's word.

orig.note: French, Montaigne's word in Of Solitude: the back shop, the room behind the counter.

carryVoice: Your line: love the front; keep a room behind it. If someone knocks, the front of the shop is still open. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Essays 1.39, Of Solitude (reserve a back shop all our own, entirely free; have spouse, children, goods and health if we can, but not so bound that our happiness depends on them; leaving the crowd is not enough; the greatest thing is to know how to belong to oneself)
